name: Rafael Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew building and repairing power lines for the electricity company, though I am still on the truck with everyone else. I am fifty-eight, and my two-year technical diploma helps when a drawing and a damaged pole disagree. I like teaching the next worker to spot a bad isolation point; I do not like the team lead responsibility on a wage that is low for this trade. My partner and I have grown children, and retirement feels close without the money to make it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a small paperwork tool does not change who tests the line. I use AI once in a while for a tidy report, but our field sheet still has to match the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am already worried about money. We have less than a month of expenses saved, few nearby lineworker jobs and a lower-than-usual wage, even though I lead difficult repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew lead shifts and check any drafted report against the signed field sheet. This month I would bring my rota and pay slips to the union pay meeting and ask for the lead rate to reflect the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, as before the AI talk. A neat AI report cannot pay the line crew lead rate my household is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show at the pay meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the callouts I led, the isolation checks I signed and the rate on each pay slip. The union can make a stronger case with those records than with my annoyance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the rate stays the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the shifts because the few nearby vacancies do not pay our bills until one becomes a real offer. My partner and I would postpone replacing the sitting-room sofa, not borrow for it.

say: A **little** AI may tidy reports, but the crew still tests every line.
I would **ask** the union to review the pay for lead responsibility.
think: **Thin** savings and low pay make our living insecure even without major AI change.
**Few** nearby jobs leave little room to walk away from a poor rate.
do: **Keep** crew lead shifts and verify drafted reports against signed field sheets.
**Take** rota and pay slips to union pay meeting this month.
feel: **Anxious** about existing household finances, with little added AI threat.
S0.quote: A neat AI report cannot pay the line crew lead rate my household is missing.
fieldNote: He **already** uses AI occasionally, yet checks reports against physical field records.
The **baseline** worry is thin savings and underpayment for senior responsibility, not technology.

steps.text: Keep line crew lead shifts and verify drafted reports
Bring rota and pay slips to union pay meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI dispatch might get a crew to the right street faster, but it must leave enough paid time for isolation. I would ask the union safety group to compare real callouts with the new schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office takes the first change, while my hands still fix lines. But a company chasing faster figures could cut our callout hours, and our savings would not cover even one month of lost wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the assigned and actual isolation time on every storm callout for six weeks. In the first year I would take that record to the union safety group, request a paid correction process and keep leading repairs while the scheduling rule is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because even a small loss of paid hours reaches our kitchen quickly. A power line schedule that cuts the isolation minutes also cuts the wage I use for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record when isolation runs long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the work order, damaged section, crew size and minutes needed to make it safe. A vague complaint is easy to dismiss, but a signed site record is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first if hours tighten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger lineworkers on shorter callouts would be first in my mind. I would ask the union group to compare their paid hours as well as mine.

say: **AI** schedules must count paid isolation time on actual line repairs.
I would **take** signed timing records to the union safety group.
think: **Office** tasks change first, but tighter callout hours could cut my already low income.
**Savings** below one month give our household little time to adjust.
do: **Log** assigned and actual isolation time for six weeks.
**Bring** signed callout records to union safety group for paid corrections.
**Keep** leading physical repairs while scheduling rule is tested.
feel: **Anxious** about a small hours loss reaching household bills quickly.
S1.quote: A power line schedule that cuts the isolation minutes also cuts the wage I use for groceries.
fieldNote: He **frames** safety time as paid time, exposing the link between crew practice and household income.
He **worries** about junior workers too, while not claiming robots have arrived in this scenario.

steps.text: Log six weeks of assigned and actual isolation time
Bring records to union safety group for paid correction rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that full thinking AI by 2028 may redraw our repair plans, and capable line robots around 2031 may take the climbs. A worker must be paid and authorised to stop a robot when the pole does not match its plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company to cut a large share of our lead callouts once robots can repair lines at sixty-three. We have less than a month saved and few other line jobs nearby; I have been waking at night over what we would live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit with my partner this week and cancel our paid sports package to protect food and heating money. Before 2028 I would ask the union to bargain for an hours floor and paid field training; after thinking AI arrives, if my shifts fall, I would ask the company for a written paid ground-check assignment before accepting less work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and the date makes my stomach tighten. A robot can take a power line climb in 2031; my household cannot skip the food bill until training starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company to pay you for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ground checker should verify isolation markers, inspect damaged hardware and have authority to stop the robot. I would need the rate and hours in writing before relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the lead callouts might shrink, but I would not ask them to fund our household without knowing their own bills. My partner and I would show them the budget only if we needed help.

say: **Thinking** AI could change plans by 2028, with capable line robots around 2031.
I would **push** for paid human stop authority and a protected hours floor.
think: I **expect** a large loss of lead callout income by sixty-three.
**Thin** savings and few local jobs make the gap frightening enough to disturb sleep.
do: **Cancel** paid sports package after reviewing household bills.
**Ask** union to bargain for hours floor and paid field training before 2028.
**Request** written paid ground-check assignment if shifts fall after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected income loss and waking at night over bills.
S2.quote: A robot can take a power line climb in 2031; my household cannot skip the food bill until training starts.
fieldNote: The **fast** scenario turns a possible technology shift into an expected large pay loss for him.
He **asks** for paid ground duties rather than counting an unfunded course as retraining.

steps.text: Cancel paid sports package to protect food and heating bills
Ask union for protected lineworker hours and paid field training
Request paid ground-check assignment if lead shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2031 could alter dispatch when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 could reach the pole at sixty-six. The company has a few years to let workers prove an inspection route on real faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and crew lead years could fit a paid field safety job, but our thin savings rule out unpaid study. A field inspection certificate will not feed my partner while the power line company leaves the course unpaid. At sixty-six I may still need wages because no retirement figure has shown we can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union training group this year for the company’s inspection course rate and posted vacancies. If a paid hands-on course and a local inspection role covering our living costs appear, I would enroll before 2031 and apply after the role is posted; otherwise I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the extra years give me a workable way to check offers. I can learn a proven physical job if the family can still buy groceries while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the inspection course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want damaged poles, isolation errors and a real crew leader able to correct me. A screen demonstration would not make me competent to sign a line safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer has only an unpaid course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decline it and stay on paid shifts. The union group could keep pressing for paid training, but I cannot use our emergency money for the company’s course.

say: The **years** to 2034 allow paid field inspection training before robots reach lines.
I would **demand** real faults and proper crew supervision in training.
think: **Diploma** and lead work may transfer, but unpaid study is impossible with thin savings.
**Retirement** at sixty-six cannot be assumed to cover living costs.
do: **Ask** union group for inspection course pay and posted vacancy terms.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course paid and local job covers living costs.
**Apply** for posted local inspection role if wage covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** but able to check a funded field path over several years.
S3.quote: A field inspection certificate will not feed my partner while the power line company leaves the course unpaid.
fieldNote: He is **willing** to change duties after proof, but the course must pay during learning.
His **age** makes retirement relevant, yet no payment amount or guaranteed exit is invented.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if inspection course paid and suitable local role posted
Apply for posted local inspector job if wage covers household bills
Keep crew lead shifts if paid inspection route is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger workers that full thinking AI in 2036 arrives when I am sixty-eight, with capable robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. I would want the electricity company to keep a paid human safety lead on each robot crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might let us build a proper retirement fund if wages improve, but I cannot count on it from less than one month saved today. I may still need work at sixty-eight, perhaps supervising isolation from the ground rather than climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take my pay records to the union wage meeting this year and ask for a rate that reflects lead duties. If the rate rises, I would put fifty from each pay packet into new retirement savings; after 2036 I would apply for a posted paid ground lead role if my retirement income still falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current cash, even with a long warning. A decade before line robots is useful only if my crew lead wage buys a cushion along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose between climbing and a ground role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written ground wage with our bills and my ability to work safely. A title alone would not keep the lights on at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why make the wage case now rather than wait for robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family needs a fair lead rate in the current job, before any machine arrives. Waiting ten years would waste years when a little extra from each pay packet could build savings.

say: A **decade** allows paid human safety lead planning before robots arrive around 2039.
I would **press** for a fair lead rate now, before any machine arrives.
think: At **sixty-eight** I may still need paid work because current savings are under one month.
A **future** retirement cushion depends on improved wages, not a guaranteed payment.
do: **Take** lead rota and pay records to union wage meeting this year.
**Save** fifty from each pay packet if lead wage rises.
**Apply** for posted paid ground lead role after 2036 if retirement income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about present cash despite the long transition.
S4.quote: A decade before line robots is useful only if my crew lead wage buys a cushion along the way.
fieldNote: His **first** move remains collective wage bargaining rooted in existing underpayment.
**New** saving is conditional on a real pay rise; current cash is not relabelled as saving.

steps.text: Take lead pay records to union wage meeting
Save fifty from each pay packet if lead rate rises
Apply for posted paid ground lead job if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect line robots around 2031 to take much of the lead callout pay before I have retirement money. A written hours floor, paid field training and a real ground-check wage would help. I cannot send a robot to buy groceries for my partner while my lineworker pay is missing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why a skilled crew lead reaches fifty-eight with less than a month saved. The lower rate and gaps between callouts have left little room after ordinary bills. I want fair pay before anyone offers me a speech about future training.

headlineQuote: I cannot send a robot to buy groceries for my partner while my lineworker pay is missing.
portrait: **Rafael** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a two-year technical diploma and strong hands-on safety judgment.
His **lower** lineworker pay, savings below one month and few nearby jobs make retirement uncertain for him and his partner.
He **uses** AI occasionally, checks its reports against field sheets and asks his union to defend paid isolation and training time.
**Fast** robots make him fear major callout loss; slower timelines open a paid inspection path only with real wages and local work.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring robots around 2031 and remove much of his lead callout income before retirement is funded.
whatWouldHelp: A **protected** hours floor, paid field training and written ground-check wages would help him keep earning safely.
